newsitem.title: GREECE: PRESS DIGEST - GREEK FINANCIAL NEWS UPDATE - JULY 14.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - GREEK FINANCIAL NEWS UPDATE - JULY 14.

text.p: Leading stories in the Greek financial press:

--The finance ministry is reportedly planning changes to the way tax is calculated on the ownership of cars and yachts. Apart from taking into account horsepower or yacht length, the ministry is now considering factoring market cost and maintenance costs into the total, in an attempt to ease the burden on those with inexpensive vehicles or boats and to tighten the screws on those with luxury cars and yachts.

--The Capital Market Commission has placed "serious obstacles" to the activity of institutional investors in derivatives, according to reports, in an attempt to regulate types of mutual fund and investment firm activity in derivatives markets.
--Greek shipowners have placed orders worth one billion dollars over the past four weeks, with the largest being a 250 million dollar cruiseship ordered by Festival Cruises.

--Personnel costs at Olympic Airways, Greece's national carrier, have spiralled upwards in the last half-year, just as OA attempts to find the capital to implement its billion drachma procurements programme for new airplanes and to finance the move to the new international airport at Spata. According to figures for June 1997, personnel costs increased from between 20-70 percent compared to December 1996, with an average increase of 30 percent. The company's wage bill is up by a conservative estimate of 36.6 percent - this figure does not include overtime, bonuses, expenses and pension fund contributions. Costs are expected to take off further in August when the third stage of an agreement between OA and the employees' union comees into effect. Estimated put OA 115 billion drachmas over its forecast spending on wages by the end of the year.

--National Bank of Greece is working feverishly to prepare for its 100 billion drachma share capital increase, set to go ahead November 15. Merrill Lynch and SBC Warburg have been appointed to handle the issue in the US and Europe. Preparation for the simultaneous conversation of a 1992 bond loan into shares is also well under way.

--Last week's signing of an agreement on principles governing relations between Greece and Turkey has given the green light to investment activity in Greece by major international financiers. Representatives of US firm Merrill Lyunch and France's Societe General reportedly visited the national economy ministry on Thursday to discuss financial prospects raised by the signing of the agreement at Madrid. However, the government is less effusive, mindful of the past failures at Greek-Turkish rapprochment at Davos.

--Corporate taxes will be lower next year, Deputy Finance Minister George Drys said. Greece has one of the highest taxes on companies, Drys admitted, and this was an active disincentive for investment.

--The president of the Federation of Greek Industries Jason Stratos has charged that "foreign pressure" is being exerted to avoid Greek industries getting one trillion drachmas worth of procurements contracts with state-run organisations and enterprises (DEKOs).

--Although there's great diversity in the sort of remuneration paid to managing directors of leading listed Greek industrial concerns, they share the fact that they get paid less than their counterparts in the banking sector and certainly less than the European average.

--Traditionally, the Athens Stock Excahnge sees a high level of activity in sleepy and hot August: foreign investors told Imerisia that they were playing the waiting game, awaiting developments in economic indicators and half-yearly company reports.
